curation.lead:
Erin Nealy Cox served as U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Texas from November 2017 through January 9, 2021 — a Trump appointee with a background in federal cybercrime prosecution, private-sector cybersecurity consulting at Stroz Friedberg (2008–2016), and a brief senior advisor role at McKinsey [Finding #3116]. On January 7, 2021 — her last day before her resignation took effect — her office filed case 4:21-cr-00005 (NDTX): a deferred prosecution agreement with The Boeing Company charging one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States in connection with the 737 MAX MCAS system and the deaths of 346 people in two crashes [Finding #3117]. The DPA imposed a $2.51 billion total financial obligation but required no guilty plea, no convicted executive, and — atypically — no independent compliance monitor; the case was filed in NDTX despite Boeing having no Texas corporate presence, a venue choice that Columbia Law professor John Coffee publicly characterized as suspicious [Finding #3117].

Five months after the Boeing DPA was signed, Kirkland & Ellis announced Nealy Cox as a new partner in its Dallas office. The K&E press release was personally authored by Mark Filip, the K&E partner who had signed the DPA on Boeing's behalf as lead defense counsel — meaning the prosecutor and her principal opposing counsel became law firm colleagues within a single calendar year [Finding #3124]. Filip had also served as DOJ Deputy Attorney General in 2008–2009 and is the author of the "Filip Factors" — the formal DOJ guidelines governing when deferred prosecution agreements are appropriate — which he has since deployed on behalf of corporate clients at Kirkland & Ellis [Finding #3124]. Boeing victims' families initially filed claims of impropriety regarding the transition; those claims were withdrawn on January 20, 2022 [Finding #3124].

The Boeing DPA was breached in May 2024 after the January 2024 Alaska Airlines door-plug blowout, and the full case cycle — DPA filed January 2021, breach finding May 2024, replacement non-prosecution agreement May 2025, dismissal November 2025 — concluded without a criminal conviction [Finding #3118]. Commentators and victims' advocate attorney Paul Cassell drew a structural parallel to the 2008 Jeffrey Epstein non-prosecution agreement negotiated by Trump-appointed U.S. Attorney Alexander Acosta, in which Kirkland & Ellis partners also represented the defense; in both instances a Republican-appointed U.S. Attorney negotiated an agreement widely criticized as lenient, with K&E on the defense side, and resigned shortly thereafter — the American Prospect headlined its 2024 analysis "The Boeing Epstein Deal" [Finding #3122].

sections.title: Career Background
sections.content: Nealy Cox was born in 1970 in Pascagoula, Mississippi. She earned a BBA from the University of Texas at Austin and a JD magna cum laude from SMU Dedman School of Law, then clerked for Judge Henry Politz on the Fifth Circuit and Judge Barefoot Sanders in NDTX. She joined Simpson Thacher briefly (1996–97) before entering the NDTX U.S. Attorney's office as an AUSA in 1999, where she handled cybercrime and white-collar matters through 2008 — including a detachment to DOJ Main Justice in 2004–05 as chief of staff to the Assistant Attorney General for the Office of Legal Policy [Finding #3116]. She spent 2008–2016 at Stroz Friedberg, a digital forensics and cybersecurity consultancy, as an executive. A one-year stint as a senior advisor at McKinsey preceded her nomination as U.S. Attorney for NDTX on September 22, 2017; she was confirmed November 9 and sworn in November 17 of that year [Finding #3116]. She is a Federalist Society contributor and serves on the board of Sally Beauty Holdings [Finding #3116].

sections.title: The Boeing 737 MAX Deferred Prosecution Agreement
sections.content:
Case 4:21-cr-00005, filed in NDTX on January 7, 2021, charged The Boeing Company with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States in connection with the fraudulent representations made to the FAA regarding the 737 MAX MCAS flight control system — the system implicated in the Lion Air Flight 610 crash (October 2018, 189 deaths) and the Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crash (March 2019, 157 deaths), 346 total deaths [Finding #3117]. The DPA was assigned to Judge Reed O'Connor in NDTX. The financial terms totaled $2.51 billion: $243.6 million criminal penalty, $500 million victim compensation fund, and $1.77 billion in airline customer compensation. No individual Boeing executive was charged. Boeing entered no guilty plea. No independent compliance monitor was required, which legal commentators characterized as atypical for an agreement of this magnitude [Finding #3117]. The case was brought in NDTX despite Boeing's lack of Texas corporate presence; Professor Coffee publicly questioned the venue selection [Finding #3117].

The DOJ case record (EFTA00040903 and related Morning Digests in the DugganUSA corpus) documents Nealy Cox's active role as NDTX U.S. Attorney during the preceding period, including a July 30, 2020 tax fraud prosecution attributed to her office [Finding #3127]. The CourtListener docket (29089563) lists Chad Meacham as the lead line prosecutor, with Mark Filip of Kirkland & Ellis signing for Boeing on the defense side; former NDTX U.S. Attorney Richard Roper III also appeared [Finding #3127]. Nealy Cox's resignation took effect on January 9, 2021 — two days after the DPA was filed [Finding #3117].

The DPA was found breached on May 14, 2024 — DOJ determined Boeing had failed to implement the required compliance program under paragraphs 21, 22, and 26(d). The breach was triggered in part by the January 5, 2024 Alaska Airlines door-plug blowout. A proposed plea deal was rejected by Judge O'Connor on December 5, 2024 over objections to the monitor-selection process. A replacement non-prosecution agreement was reached on May 23, 2025: $444.5 million victim fund and $240 million criminal fine, with Boeing hiring its own outside contractor rather than a court-appointed monitor. Judge O'Connor dismissed the case on November 6, 2025. Victims' families filed Fifth Circuit mandamus petitions on November 13, 2025. The complete cycle — DPA January 2021 through NPA dismissal November 2025 — concluded without a criminal conviction [Finding #3118].

sections.title: Transition to Kirkland & Ellis
sections.content:
On June 23, 2021 — five months after the Boeing DPA was filed — Kirkland & Ellis announced Nealy Cox as a new partner in its Dallas office. The K&E press release was personally authored by Mark Filip, who had led the Boeing defense and signed the DPA on Boeing's behalf, and also by Andrew Calder, a K&E Houston partner and executive committee member, who cited his "personal experience" with her [Finding #3124]. Nealy Cox began at K&E on September 1, 2021, practicing in government regulatory and internal investigations — the work that defends against the type of prosecution she previously conducted [Finding #3124]. Corporate Crime Reporter headlined its coverage: "Lead Boeing Prosecutor Joins Boeing Corporate Criminal Defense Firm Kirkland Ellis" [Finding #3124].

Professor Coffee's characterization — that the U.S. Attorney joining the defense counsel's firm "suggests they were both on the same wavelength" — was widely quoted in legal press coverage of the transition [Finding #3124]. Boeing victims' families filed claims of impropriety, which were withdrawn on January 20, 2022 [Finding #3124]. The sequence is documented: DPA filed January 7, 2021; resignation effective January 9, 2021; K&E announcement June 23, 2021; K&E start date September 1, 2021 [Findings #3117, #3124].

The K&E–DOJ revolving door that Nealy Cox's transition illustrates is documented more broadly in the network: Mark Filip authored the "Filip Factors" as Deputy AG (2008–09) before returning to K&E and deploying those same criteria on behalf of Boeing, BP, Volkswagen, and Goldman Sachs; K&E partner Brian Benczkowski moved in the opposite direction — K&E to head of DOJ Criminal Division — and then back to Boeing as VP/Assistant General Counsel in September 2025 [Finding #3124].

sections.title: Structural Parallel: Acosta and the Epstein NPA
sections.content:
Attorney Paul Cassell — victims' advocate in both the Epstein and Boeing cases — publicly drew the comparison between the two agreements. Both involved Trump-appointed U.S. Attorneys who negotiated agreements that legal commentators characterized as historically lenient for the magnitude of the conduct. Both had Kirkland & Ellis on the defense side: K&E partners Jay Lefkowitz and Ken Starr negotiated Alexander Acosta's 2008 Epstein non-prosecution agreement; K&E partner Mark Filip signed the 2021 Boeing DPA. Both U.S. Attorneys resigned shortly after their respective agreements. Acosta became Labor Secretary and resigned in July 2019 when the Epstein NPA received renewed scrutiny; Nealy Cox resigned January 9, 2021 and joined K&E [Finding #3122]. The American Prospect titled its February 9, 2024 analysis "The Boeing Epstein Deal" [Finding #3122].

One documented difference: Acosta was himself a former K&E associate prior to his government service; Nealy Cox had no prior K&E affiliation before the Boeing matter [Finding #3122]. The parallel is a synthesis-level inference based on structural features of the two agreements and documented statements by Cassell and media commentators; it does not rest on any documented communication between the two matters or the two U.S. Attorneys [Finding #3122, confidence: medium].

sections.title: Political Contributions
sections.content: FEC Schedule A filings show Nealy Cox — listing her address as 3432 Southwestern Blvd, Dallas TX 75225 and her employer as Kirkland Ellis — made the following federal contributions while a K&E partner: $8,300 to the Vance Victory joint fundraising committee (split between JD Vance for Senate and Working for Ohio PAC) on April 5, 2024 (FEC committees C00817072 and C00783142); $1,000 to Never Surrender Inc, a Trump leadership PAC, on October 31, 2024 (committee C00828541); $2,900 to Christina Nolan for U.S. Senate (VT-R) on April 27, 2022, and $1,000 on January 29, 2022 (committee C00800532) [Finding #3120]. The Nolan donation is notable because Nolan was herself a Trump-appointed U.S. Attorney (District of Vermont) — a K&E partner contributing to a former U.S. Attorney running for Senate [Finding #3120]. All recorded donations are to Republican candidates and committees [Finding #3120].

open_questions: What was the precise timeline of K&E recruitment contacts with Nealy Cox relative to the DPA negotiation? The public record establishes that Filip welcomed her five months after the DPA was signed, but the date any employment discussion was first initiated has not been documented.

Why was the Boeing case filed in NDTX — a district with no Boeing corporate presence — rather than in WDWA (Boeing's headquarters) or the NDIL (Boeing's Chicago office, home district of K&E's flagship office)? Professor Coffee raised the venue question publicly but no DOJ explanation has been documented.

The original DPA waived the independent compliance monitor requirement — an atypical provision for a case of this scale. Who at DOJ, and at what level, approved that waiver? The line prosecutor was Chad Meacham; it is not documented whether the no-monitor decision was made at the AUSA level, the U.S. Attorney level, or required Main Justice approval.

The Boeing victims' families withdrew their impropriety claims against Nealy Cox on January 20, 2022. The terms, if any, under which those claims were withdrawn have not been made public. Whether the withdrawal was a litigation settlement or a unilateral decision is not documented in available records.

Nealy Cox's Stroz Friedberg tenure (2008–2016) overlaps with the period when Stroz Friedberg was conducting sensitive investigations for major financial institutions and law firms. Whether any Stroz clients later appeared in the Boeing matter or the K&E network has not been investigated.

applicable_models.rationale: The K&E–DOJ revolving door documented here — Filip writing DPA policy as Deputy AG, then using it to defend Boeing at K&E, then welcoming the Boeing prosecutor as a K&E partner — is a canonical instance of the Private Order model's "revolving door as access mechanism" and "institutional capture" mechanisms. The network includes Nealy Cox as a node in the Filip → K&E → DOJ Criminal Division cluster documented in that model.

The factual record positions Nealy Cox at a documentable point on the enabler gradient. She oversaw a prosecution that legal commentators characterized as capturing lenient terms for Boeing, then joined the defense firm within months. Whether that reflects knowing participation, willful blindness, or professional conduct consistent with DOJ norms is the specific question the gradient model is designed to frame — the platform should present the evidence and let the reader assess.
